title: A small edge, many generations
hook: No beetle ever changes colour. So how does the whole population change?

knows: offspring tend to resemble their parents
predators eat prey that they can see

misconception: A small survival advantage makes only a small difference, and populations change because individuals change (adapt) during their lives.
objective: The learner can explain that a heritable edge is applied again every generation, so a small edge compounds (from 1% to about 99% in 100 generations at a 10% edge in this model), and that the population changes because the mix of who leaves young changes, not because any individual changes.

claims.text: In this model (young always share their parent's colour, generations do not overlap, a very large population so chance plays no part, and dark beetles leave a fixed share more young than pale ones), the ratio of dark to pale beetles is multiplied by (1 + edge) every generation.
claims.source: Haploid selection recursion with discrete, non-overlapping generations: p' = p w / (p w + 1 - p), so p'/(1-p') = w p/(1-p). Gillespie (2004), Population Genetics: A Concise Guide, 2nd ed., ch. 3; Hartl & Clark (2007), Principles of Population Genetics, 4th ed., ch. 5. v2 adds non-overlapping generations (fact-check F4).

claims.text: With a 10% edge and 1% dark at the start, dark beetles are about 99% of the population after 100 generations.
With the same 10% edge, dark beetles stay under 10% for the first 25 generations and pass half the population at about generation 49.
With a 1% edge, the same 100 generations only take dark beetles from 1% to about 3%.
claims.source: odds = (1/99) x 1.01^100 = 0.0273, so p = 0.0266 (about 3%). v2: arithmetic in this source corrected (fact-check F1); claim text unchanged.

claims.text: No individual changes colour in natural selection; the population changes because more of each new generation is descended from the parents that survived and bred.
claims.source: Futuyma & Kirkpatrick (2017), Evolution, 4th ed.; misconception documented in Bishop & Anderson (1990), 'Student conceptions of natural selection and its role in evolution', Journal of Research in Science Teaching 27(5): 415-427. v2: chapter number dropped (fact-check F2); claim text unchanged.

claims.text: Around Manchester, the dark form of the peppered moth was first recorded in 1848 and made up about 98% of the population there by 1895, roughly one generation per year.
claims.source: Cook (2003), 'The rise and fall of the carbonaria form of the peppered moth', Quarterly Review of Biology 78(4): 399-417; Majerus (1998), Melanism: Evolution in Action, Oxford University Press.

claims.text: Real populations are finite, so chance can remove a rare helpful variant before selection spreads it; the model on the stage leaves this out.
claims.source: Haldane (1927) fixation probability approx. 2s for a new beneficial mutation; Gillespie (2004), ch. 3.

claims.text: In the model, 1.1 multiplied by itself 100 times is about 14,000 (1.1^100 = 13,781), so a starting ratio of 1 dark to 99 pale (the ratio shown on the stage) becomes about 139 dark to 1 pale, which is about 99 in 100. The stage message shows the dark-to-pale ratio and the 1.1 multiplier each generation.
claims.source: 1.1^100 = 13,780.6; (1/99) x 13,780.6 = 139.2; 139.2 / 140.2 = 0.9929. Demo.tsx computes GROWTH, RATIO_AT_100 and AT_100 from darkShare(), the function that draws the stage.

claims.text: Selection needs many generations rather than a big edge: with a 1% edge starting from 1% dark, dark beetles take about 462 generations to pass half the population.
claims.source: Reveal: "selection needs time, not a big edge". odds = (1/99) x 1.01^g > 1 first at g = 462 (fact-checker script). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: If one type of seed survives drought 5% more often than another and seeds inherit their parent's type, the first type's share keeps growing generation after generation, even if it starts rare; no plant changes type.
claims.source: Recall card in meta.json. Same recursion as c1 with w = 1.05: the A:B ratio is multiplied by 1.05 each generation (assumes the 5% is a constant relative advantage in leaving offspring, large population, no other forces). Added by fact-checker 2026-10-12; needs an independent check.

claims.text: In this lesson's made-up scenario, birds spot pale beetles more easily on sooty bark, which is why dark beetles leave more young.
claims.source: Scenario stated in the predict question (v2, learner finding 7). The mechanism mirrors bird predation on peppered moths (Cook, Grant, Saccheri & Mallet (2012), 'Selective bird predation on the peppered moth: the last experiment of Michael Majerus', Biology Letters 8: 609-612), but the beetles and the 10% figure are invented.

claims.text: On the stage, 100 beetles stand for a very large population, and each generation shown is entirely new beetles.
claims.source: Demo.tsx: the grid shows round(100 x share) dark beetles; stage label v2 "Model: 100 beetles stand for a huge population. Each generation is all new." (learner finding 3, label-the-model-on-the-stage).

recall.question: Plant A's seeds survive drought 5% more often than plant B's, and seeds inherit their parent's type. A starts rare. Over many generations of droughts, what happens?
options: A stays rare: 5% is too small to matter
A becomes common, because the 5% edge repeats every generation
Each B plant slowly turns into an A plant
recall.why: The edge multiplies the A:B ratio again every generation, so even a small edge compounds. No plant changes type; A plants just leave more seeds.
